title: The ten days
hook: no days are dearer to Allah for good deeds than the first ten of Dhul Hijjah (Bukhari)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Six of Shawwal, and your line was six more. Which small Ramadan habit did you keep going for one more day? Day five hundred thirteen.

Ramadan is usually the month that comes to mind first when the holiest days of the Islamic year come up, and its nights carry Laylat al-Qadr. But a hadith in Bukhari points somewhere else. It names a different stretch of days, about two months after Ramadan ends, at the start of the last month of the year, the month of pilgrimage. While pilgrims are heading for Mecca, everyone else, at home, is also in a season. Today: the ten days.

In Sahih al-Bukhari, Ibn 'Abbas reports that the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ said there are no days in which good deeds are more beloved to God than these, meaning the first ten days of Dhul Hijjah. The companions were startled. Not even striving in the path of God? Not even that, he said, except a man who goes out with his life and his wealth and comes back with nothing. It's a striking answer. An ordinary good deed, done in these ten days, is set beside the hardest sacrifice there is. Commentators also connect the days to the Qur'an. Surah Al-Fajr opens with an oath, by the dawn, and ten nights, and commentators going back to Ibn 'Abbas understood those ten nights as these. And Surah Al-Hajj speaks of remembering God's name on appointed days, which Ibn 'Abbas is reported to have explained as the ten. What do people actually do? They do more of what they already do. Extra prayer, charity, reading, kindness. Some fast the first nine days. Others fast at least the ninth, the day of 'Arafah, when the pilgrims stand on the plain; a hadith in Sahih Muslim hopes that fast wipes away the faults of the year before and the year after. Some companions, Bukhari notes, used to walk through the markets in these days saying the takbir aloud, and people around them took it up. And a hadith in Muslim says that someone planning to offer a sacrifice for Eid shouldn't cut their hair or nails from the start of the month, a small mark in the body that the season has begun. The point isn't a new set of rules. It's a window: the same deeds, in a season when they weigh more.
screen: `NO DAYS DEARER FOR GOOD DEEDS.` · `BY THE DAWN, AND TEN NIGHTS.` · `THE FAST OF 'ARAFAH.` · `THE SAME DEEDS, A HEAVIER SEASON.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: one extra good, each day. Sit, and let the breath settle. Think of ten days, starting today. Choose one small good you could add to each of them. Not a heroic one. A text to someone who's lonely. A coin in a box. Ten minutes of reading. Picking up litter on the walk home. Pick something you can actually do ten times. Picture yourself doing it on day twelve, when you're tired. If it still fits, keep it. If you pray, you can make your intention now. The bell holds the time.
The ten days. The first ten of Dhul Hijjah, the month of pilgrimage, when, in the hadith, good deeds are dearer to God than on any other days. Today's word.
Your line: the best ten days. Today, do the first of your ten small goods, and mark it somewhere so day two remembers. Day five hundred thirteen.

howItsDone: In the first ten days of Dhul Hijjah many Muslims increase prayer, charity, remembrance and takbir; many fast the day of 'Arafah, and some fast the first nine days.

fork.setup: the Prophet has just said no days are dearer for good deeds than these ten. what do the companions ask?
options: not even striving in the path of God?
can we skip the other months, then?
do the days count if we're not in Mecca?
fork.reveal: they asked about striving in God's path. he said not even that, except one who goes out with life and wealth and returns with nothing.

original.note: Arabic: Dhul Hijjah, the month of the pilgrimage, the last month of the Hijri year.

trapdoor: what you thought: the days before Eid, a countdown.
what it means: a season when ordinary good deeds weigh more, for pilgrims and for everyone at home.
what a scholar hears: Bukhari 969 from Ibn 'Abbas; Al-Fajr 89:2's ten nights read as these by commentators from Ibn 'Abbas on; and the fast of 'Arafah in Muslim 1162.

sources.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 969 (Ibn 'Abbas: no days dearer for good deeds)
Qur'an 89:1–2 (by the dawn, and ten nights)
Sahih Muslim 1977 (hair and nails before the sacrifice)
Sahih al-Bukhari, book of the two Eids (Ibn 'Umar and Abu Hurayra's takbir in the markets, a ta'liq report)

notes: All hadith paraphrased; numbers from memory (Bukhari 969; Muslim 1162, 1977); confirm.
The reading of 89:2's ten nights as the first ten of Dhul Hijjah is the majority view among classical commentators, but others exist; stated as 'a long line of commentators'. Confirm.
Ibn 'Abbas on 22:28 'appointed days' as the ten: reported as a ta'liq in Bukhari; confirm.
The hair-and-nails ruling: schools differ on whether it is obligatory or recommended; script keeps it descriptive.
The hook says Ramadan's nights carry Laylat al-Qadr and that this hadith names different days; scholars discuss how the two compare (days vs nights). Confirm the framing is fair.
